solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Tags celebrity, one quitting exercises

parts.note: a big name is a famous person

indicators.note: whoever is quitting leaves, so that letter drops out of the word it was part of

parts.note: Pilates is a system of body-conditioning exercises
one as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: A famous person labels things while someone drops out of the fitness class.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tags' looks like a verb with celebrity as its subject, but it is a plural noun: labels on doors and desks.
explanation.definitionFit: Small plates bearing a person's name on doors or desks serve as identifying labels, a straightforward synonym.

clue.text: Crass family, friends and neighbours at the outset turned up

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something upward makes it read from bottom to top
the outset is the very start, so only the opening letter of each word counts

parts.note: first letter
first letter
first letter
first letter

explanation.surface: Tactless relatives and neighbours show up at the start of something.
explanation.walkthrough: The initials FFAN read upward in the down light. Naff is British slang for tacky or uncool.
explanation.definitionFit: British slang for tasteless or lacking style, close enough to crude and vulgar to work as a synonym.

clue.text: The details for workers on estate?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the practical workings of how something is done
second meaning: people who repair cars, an estate being a British station wagon

explanation.surface: Someone asks for the particulars of the staff employed on a country estate.
explanation.walkthrough: An estate here is not land but an estate car, the British name for a station wagon, which is why the question mark is there.
explanation.definitionFit: The workings or nuts and bolts of a process, and also tradespeople who service motor vehicles.

clue.text: Noble exercises for rising when received by exquisite maiden

parts.note: PE is physical education, school exercises

indicators.note: whatever is received is taken inside by the receiver

parts.note: ethereal means delicate and exquisitely light

indicators.note: in a down entry something rising reads from the bottom upward

parts.note: taken as written
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: An aristocrat's workout regime is taken up by a lovely young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: The maiden is not a young woman but a cricket term: a maiden over is one in which no runs are scored, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: A member of the British nobility entitled to sit in the House of Lords, so a titled aristocrat.

clue.text: Damn charger lifting tail

indicators.note: raising the final letter in a down entry moves it higher up the word

parts.note: one who charges someone with a crime

explanation.surface: A cavalry horse flicks its tail up; someone swears.
explanation.walkthrough: The final R of ACCUSER is lifted two places, past E and S. 'Charger' tempts you toward a horse; here it is a person who charges.
explanation.definitionFit: To curse or call down damnation on someone, a formal verb synonym of the imperative 'damn'.

clue.text: Shows hosted by Angevin, c'est-à-dire

indicators.note: a host holds guests inside, so the letters sit within the following words

parts.note: the run of letters straddles the proper name and the French phrase

explanation.surface: A French phrase meaning 'that is to say', used by a medieval Angevin king to present entertainments.
explanation.walkthrough: The Angevins were the Plantagenet kings from Anjou; c'est-à-dire is French for 'that is to say'. The answer runs from inside Angevin into c'est.
explanation.definitionFit: To evince is to display or reveal a quality clearly, a formal synonym for show in the third person.

clue.text: Take lead from great boss

indicators.note: the lead is the first letter, and taking it away leaves the rest

parts.note: jumbo means huge

explanation.surface: Follow the example set by an impressive manager.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boss' looks like a manager but means the raised knob at the centre of a shield, which is what an umbo is.
explanation.definitionFit: An umbo is the central projecting stud of a shield, which is also called a boss in the ornamental sense.

clue.text: Nice day for reporting religious leader

indicators.note: reporting is passing on by word of mouth, so the spoken form is what counts

parts.note: mardi is French for Tuesday, a day in the French city of Nice

explanation.surface: A pleasant day to report on a cleric.
explanation.walkthrough: Nice is the French city, so its day is French: MARDI, which in a non-rhotic British accent sounds like the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: In Islamic belief the Mahdi is the prophesied redeemer and spiritual guide who will appear before the end of time.

clue.text: General depot, but not housing, developed in Seville cover-up?

indicators.note: something developed has been worked into a new form

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: stripping away the housing removes the outer shell and keeps the contents

parts.note: the word without its first and last letters

explanation.surface: A military commander's store, minus its buildings, is developed in the Spanish city of Seville.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitalised General looks like a rank but is only fodder. Seville oranges are the bitter kind used for marmalade.
explanation.definitionFit: The skin of a Seville orange is literally the covering of that fruit, playfully called a cover-up.

clue.text: Handle collection

parts.note: surface reading: a set of door or drawer grips
setter's reading: a handle is a name, so this is a book full of signed names

explanation.walkthrough: 'Handle' can be slang for a name, as in a CB radio handle, and a signature is a written name.
explanation.definitionFit: A book in which fans gather signatures of famous people, each signature being a person's written name.

clue.text: Small film of chief criminal

indicators.note: something criminal is bent or crooked, so the letters are twisted out of shape

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A short movie about a gang boss.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chief criminal' reads as a crime boss; 'criminal' is really the signal to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiche is a sheet of microfilm holding tiny photographed pages, so a small piece of film.

clue.text: A canine companion I must follow: one impressing audibly

indicators.note: one thing following another means it is placed after it

parts.note: CH is Companion of Honour, a British order
taken as written

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so the spoken sound counts, not the spelling

parts.note: someone who wows people, said in a non-rhotic accent

explanation.surface: A dog-owner's pet sticks close behind as they try to impress.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the tiny dog breed; 'canine companion' looks like one phrase, but the definition stops at 'A canine'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Chihuahua is a very small breed of dog originating in Mexico, so an example of a canine.

clue.text: When to pay for past 24 hours of audit?

parts.note: a day lasts 24 hours
taken as written
a reckoning is a calculation of accounts

explanation.surface: A question about when a day's worth of accountancy should be billed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pay for past' sounds like settling an invoice, but it means being punished for earlier misdeeds.
explanation.definitionFit: The time when someone must face the consequences of earlier wrongdoing, idiomatically paying for their sins.

clue.text: Dance, lifting bottom in mock revelation

indicators.note: something in something else sits inside it
in a down entry, raising the lowest letter moves it to the top

parts.note: the calypso is a Caribbean dance and song style
to ape is to mimic or mock

explanation.surface: A cheeky dance move of raising one's backside is a comical unveiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottom' is not a backside but the last letter of a word written downwards, which is why the move only works in a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Apocalypse comes from the Greek for uncovering; the Book of Revelation is also called the Apocalypse.

clue.text: Love-potion, extremely acidic, taken by Ulstermen off and on

parts.note: a pH of 1 is strongly acidic, written PH plus I for one

indicators.note: switching off and on means taking every other one in turn

parts.note: the second, fourth, sixth and eighth letters

explanation.surface: Northern Irishmen intermittently drink a sour love drug.
explanation.walkthrough: The chemistry reading is the trick: pH measures acidity, and pH 1 is right at the acidic extreme. Ulster is Northern Ireland.
explanation.definitionFit: A philtre is a drink supposed to arouse romantic desire in whoever takes it, a magic potion.

clue.text: Disaster team stopping to drink

indicators.note: a stopper plugs the inside of a bottle, so one piece sits in the other

parts.note: to sup is to drink in sips
a crew is a team of workers

explanation.surface: Catastrophe: the side quits in order to go drinking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stopping' reads as ceasing, but here it means plugging a gap.
explanation.definitionFit: A screw-up is informal for a botched mess or fiasco, a colloquial word for a calamity.

clue.text: Yawned, struggling to eat too much chicken

indicators.note: eating takes something inside
something struggling is thrashing about and out of order

parts.note: taken as written
OTT is over the top

explanation.surface: Someone yawned while struggling to eat more chicken than was sensible.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Too much chicken' looks like one phrase; the definition is the last word only. OTT, over the top, is British shorthand for excessive.
explanation.definitionFit: The Wyandotte is an American breed of domestic fowl, so a specific example of a chicken.

clue.text: Nuts about old exhibit, sculptor's first

parts.note: CA is circa, about
shew is an archaic spelling of show

indicators.note: first means only the opening letter of that word is kept

parts.note: first letter

explanation.surface: Someone is crazy about an antique display, the sculptor's leading piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts about' reads as crazy about; 'Nuts' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Cashews are kidney-shaped tropical seeds eaten as snacks and sold as a common kind of nut.

clue.text: False report by Brit, maybe doffing cap

indicators.note: doffing a cap removes the top, and the top of a down word is its first letter

parts.note: Britons live on an island, so a Brit is one example of an islander

explanation.surface: A British person tipping their hat has made up a story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' flags that a Brit is only one kind of islander.
explanation.definitionFit: Slander is spoken defamation, an untrue and damaging statement about someone.

clue.text: Make up for mistake by Head introducing one

parts.note: an X marks an error, and here the letter is spelt out

indicators.note: to introduce is to bring something in, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: pate is an old word for the head
one as the Roman numeral I

explanation.surface: Atone for an error committed by the headteacher when bringing someone in.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital H makes Head look like a headteacher. The letter X is written out as EX, the way you would say it.
explanation.definitionFit: To expiate a wrong is to atone or make amends for it, a formal synonym.

clue.text: Death tally rising after hospital goes from a local area?

parts.note: death is the end of life

indicators.note: in a down entry, rising means reading upward
whatever goes has left, so that letter drops out

parts.note: to tally or agree is to chime
H is the map abbreviation for hospital

explanation.surface: The death toll climbs after a hospital closes in a particular district.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Death tally' looks like a body count, but tally is a verb, as in figures that chime. CHIME loses H, then turns upward.
explanation.definitionFit: Endemic describes something native to or regularly found in a particular region or population.

clue.text: Note Universal about to secure bold double act

parts.note: la is a note of the sol-fa scale
U is the film certificate for universal viewing
re means about or concerning
to land a deal is to secure it
hardy means brave and robust

explanation.surface: Universal Pictures' memo about signing a daring comedy pair.
explanation.walkthrough: Universal hints at the film studio, which fits the scene, but it gives only the U of a British film rating.
explanation.definitionFit: Stan Laurel and Oliver Hardy were a famous comic duo of early Hollywood cinema, a classic example.

clue.text: Open University taking lead on nuclear energy

parts.note: U is the abbreviation for university

indicators.note: the lead is what goes in front, the opening letter

parts.note: first letter
zip means vigour or energy

explanation.surface: Britain's distance-learning Open University leads the way on nuclear power.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Open University' is a real British institution, but Open is the definition, detached from the name.
explanation.definitionFit: To unfasten a zipped bag or file is to open it, a specific way of opening.

clue.text: Tea-time waffle?

parts.note: cha is slang for tea
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A waffle served at afternoon tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The waffle looks like a teatime snack; the question mark flags that it is idle talk instead.
explanation.definitionFit: To waffle is to talk at length about nothing much, like light conversation or gossip.

clue.text: Bewilderment caused by this 60s rebel doing a U-turn

parts.note: this is the crossword the solver is doing

indicators.note: a U-turn sends you back the way you came, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: mods were a 1960s British youth subculture on scooters

explanation.surface: Confusion caused by a sixties rebel changing their stance entirely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' points at the thing in front of you, the crossword itself, a setter's self-reference.
explanation.definitionFit: Puzzledom is the state of being puzzled, a rare but real word for perplexity and confusion.

clue.text: Dutch painter has time for second mistake

indicators.note: having one thing for another means swapping it in as a replacement

parts.note: Hieronymus Bosch, Netherlandish painter
T is the abbreviation for time
S is the abbreviation for second

explanation.surface: A Dutch artist takes a moment to fix an error.
explanation.walkthrough: In BOSCH the S for second is replaced by T for time.
explanation.definitionFit: A botch is a clumsily bungled piece of work, a synonym for a blunder.

clue.text: Bombshell removed from casing for show

indicators.note: taking something out of its casing strips away the outer layer on both sides

parts.note: a bombshell is a very attractive woman

explanation.surface: An explosive shell is taken out of its case for display.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bombshell' suggests explosives, but it is the old slang for a glamorous woman. SEXPOT loses its outer S and T.
explanation.definitionFit: An expo is a large public exhibition, short for exposition, so a trade show.

clue.text: Lying PC number twenty-two, extremely corrupt

indicators.note: to corrupt is to spoil the proper form, jumbling the order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: extreme means at the very edge, so only the outermost letters are kept

parts.note: the first and last letters

explanation.surface: A dishonest police constable, badge number twenty-two, is thoroughly corrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lying' paints a dishonest officer, but it means lying flat. PC is police constable in the surface only; here it is just letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Procumbent means lying face down or, of plants, trailing along the ground, a botanical sense of prone.
